h1: Five first homebrew recipes in an order that teaches skills
title: Five First Homebrew Recipes in Order | Craft Beer School
desc: Five first homebrew recipes in an order that builds one new skill at a time, from an extract pale ale to a home lager.
teaser: Brew these five beers in this order and each one teaches you a skill the next one needs.
standfirst: Most new brewers pick recipes at random and learn by accident. A better plan is a sequence where each beer adds one skill. Here are five beers in an order that takes you from your first extract batch to a clean lager.
sections:
Every beer style tests a different skill. A stout tests your handling of dark malt. A lager tests temperature control and patience. A hazy IPA tests oxygen control. Brew a lager first and you face all of those at once, with no way of knowing which one went wrong.

The five beers below each add one new skill to what you already know. Brew them in order, take notes and you will have the core of homebrewing in about six months.
1. An extract pale ale: process and sanitation

Start with malt extract, hops and dry yeast. Extract removes the mash, so all your attention goes to the basics: sanitising everything on the cold side, boiling, adding hops on time, chilling, pitching and keeping fermentation at 18 to 20 °C.

Aim for an ordinary pale ale of about 1.045 and 30 IBU. If it comes out clean and drinkable, your sanitation and fermentation work. If it does not, you have learnt where to look before adding the complexity of a mash. Most first batches go wrong in the same few places. None of them is the recipe.
2. A single malt, single hop ale: your first mash

Next, go all-grain with the simplest possible recipe: one base malt and one hop. Pale ale malt with a hop such as Cascade or East Kent Goldings works well. Use brew in a bag in a single pot.

The new skill is mashing: hitting a mash temperature of about 66 °C, holding it for 60 minutes and measuring how much sugar you got out, which is your efficiency. With only one malt and one hop, you also learn exactly what each tastes like. Our 10 litre pale ale recipe is a good template at a small scale.
3. An amber ale with crystal malt: building a grist

Now add specialty malts. An amber ale of around 1.050 with pale malt, a little Munich and 5 to 10% crystal malt teaches you how colour and caramel flavour build up. It also shows the danger of too much crystal, which turns beer sweet and heavy.

This is where recipe design starts. Work out the grist yourself rather than copying a recipe: target gravity, colour and the balance of bitterness to malt. Try mashing a degree or two warmer than last time and note how the body changes.
4. A dry stout: dark malt and water

A dry stout of about 1.042 is lower in alcohol than people expect. It uses roasted barley or black malt at around 8 to 10% of the grist, with flaked barley for body and a firm bitterness.

The new skills are dark malt and water. Roasted grains add acidity to the mash, which is why dark beers often brew well with hard, alkaline water that would make a pale ale harsh. In parts of India with borewell water, a stout is often the easiest beer to get right. You also learn restraint: too much roast and the beer tastes acrid. Serve it a little warmer, around 10 to 12 °C, to taste what the malt is doing.
5. A lager: temperature control and patience

Finish with a lager, the hardest beer here. A clean helles or Pilsner of about 1.048 hides nothing. Lager yeast ferments cool, around 9 to 13 °C, then the beer needs weeks of cold conditioning near 0 to 2 °C.

In India that means a fridge or freezer with a temperature controller, which is why lager comes last. You also need a strong pitch of healthy yeast and a diacetyl rest, a couple of days at about 16 to 18 °C near the end of fermentation so the yeast can clean up buttery flavours. Our guide to brewing a lager at home walks through the set-up.
What you will know after five beers

Keep each beer's recipe and notes on one page with its tasting notes. When you rebrew any of the five later, you will be able to see how far your skills have moved. Expect each to take about a month from brew day to a drinkable beer, longer for the lager, so the five fill most of a year if you brew one at a time.

After these five, you can sanitise, mash, design a grist, handle dark malt and water. You can also control fermentation temperature. That covers most homebrew styles. Hazy IPAs, Belgian ales and sours each add a skill of their own, but none needs a new foundation.

Each brew teaches more if someone experienced tastes it and tells you what they find. That is one reason homebrewers enter competitions; our guide to entering a homebrew competition explains how. Feedback on a scoresheet often shows faults you had stopped noticing.

Your first step: order the ingredients for an extract pale ale and pick a brew date within the next two weeks.
faqs: What should my first homebrew be?
An extract pale ale with dry yeast. It lets you focus on sanitation, boiling and fermentation before adding the mash.
Why should I brew a lager last?
Lager needs cool fermentation, cold conditioning and strong yeast health. In India that means a fridge with a temperature controller.
Is stout a good beer to brew with hard water?
Often yes. Roasted grains acidify the mash, so stouts tolerate hard, alkaline water better than pale beers.
